source: FindMyPast — 1851 England, Wales & Scotland Census; England Marriages 1538-1973
census: 1851 census · Drivers Fields, St Paul, Bristol · HO107/1949, folio 478, page 14, schedule 66 · registration district Bristol, sub-district Saint Paul, ecclesiastical parish St Barnabas

marriage.line: HANNAH SANIGER married JAMES WAKEFIELD at Bristol on 17 OCTOBER 1831
marriage.means: The first English record of this marriage, and the first English record of any kind to give Hannah the surname Saniger. Until today the maiden name rested entirely on five Queensland death registrations, written down a world away and up to forty years later.

wrong.claim: Hannah Saniger was not born in Gloucestershire.
built: That all 81 Gloucestershire Saniger households could be excluded, because she was in none of them.
That her baptism lay in a Bristol nonconformist chapel — thirty-six registers catalogued, twelve named as candidates.
That Bristol's position astride the Avon mattered, and she might be a Somerset-side woman.
That a Saniger household at Oxford Road, born at CHEW MAGNA in Somerset, was the best lead this archive had ever had — a page built for it, and the parish register put first on the errand list.
wrong.rested: A single binary tick in the 1841 census: the column that asks only whether a person was born in the same county, yes or no.
wrong.beats: The 1851 census asked a different question. It asked WHERE, and the enumerator wrote BERKELEY, GLOUCESTERSHIRE — the same parish the family tree had said all along, in the same house, ten years later, about the same woman.

newFacts: James Wakefield was born at STROUD
The archive has only ever had “Gloucestershire”. Stroud is a clothing town in the same Vale as Berkeley, Dursley and Cam.
Two more children — already on this site

JABEZ, born about 1843, and ZILLAH, about 1846. When this page first went up it called them children nobody here had heard of. That was wrong: both are on the General Hewitt passenger register, published here in July, along with an EPHRAIM aged five. What is true is narrower — they are missing from the FAMILY TREE, which gives James and Hannah four children and not seven.
Miriam is a servant at ten
In the 1851 census she is already entered with an occupation. Three years later she boarded the ship as a domestic servant aged fourteen.
And the three eldest daughters are gone
Eliza, Ellen and Martha, born 1832–1836, are not in the house in 1851. Ellen was buried at five in 1840. Eliza appears in the same burial index in 1834. Martha is still open.
berkeley: The consequence runs the other way too. /berkeley has spent months explaining that FreeREG's Berkeley transcript stops in 1677 and therefore five of the tree's six Saniger generations could not be tested. FindMyPast holds Berkeley baptisms straight through the gap, with parents named — Jos 1792, Ann 1798, Jno 1803, Jno 1804, Edwd 1804, Edward 1805, Thos 1808, Victoria 1817, Eliza and Hesther 1819, Daniel 1821 — and Daniel's entry, to take one, gives his father as Edward Saniger and his mother as Kitura. The generations are testable after all. They were behind a paywall, not behind a gap in the record.

wakefield.baptism: JAMES WAKEFIELD, baptised at STROUD 6 April 1806 · father RICHARD WAKEFIELD, mother ELIZABETH WEBB.
wakefield.means: The 1851 census gave his birthplace as Stroud. Here is the baptism, in the right parish and the right year, and it opens a family this archive has never had a single name for.
wakefield.webb: And it explains something that has sat unexplained on the 1841 census for months. Living with James and Hannah at Drivers Fields, between their own children, is a two-year-old called MATILDA WEBB. James Wakefield's mother was Elizabeth Webb. The child in the house is almost certainly his kin, not a lodger's daughter.
wakefield.jabez: Jabez Wakefield's birth is registered at Bristol in 1843, which confirms the census. Neither he nor Zillah is aboard the General Hewitt in 1854, and what became of them is not yet known.
wakefield.caveat: Richard Wakefield and Elizabeth Webb are given by a FamilySearch-derived index, not yet by the parish book, and there is more than one James Wakefield in Gloucestershire. The birthplace, the year and the county all agree, which is why it is here; it is an identification, not a proof.

ellen.baptism: ELLEN WAKEFIELD, baptised at Bristol 26 OCTOBER 1834 · father JAMES WAKEFIELD, mother HANNAH — the first baptism of any of their children this archive has found.
ellen.burial: ELLEN WAKEFIELD, buried at BRISTOL, ST PAUL, PORTLAND SQUARE, 12 JULY 1840, AGED 5 · Bristol Archives, burials 1836–1855, P/St P/R/3/3.
ellen.means: This archive has said for months that three daughters — Eliza, Ellen and Martha — were not aboard the General Hewitt in 1854, and that whether they had married, followed later or stayed was unknown. Ellen did none of those things. She died at five, in her parents' own parish, ten months before the 1841 census and fourteen years before the ship.
ellen.eliza: And the same index holds an Eliza Wakefield among Bristol deaths and burials in 1834 — the year of Ellen's baptism. The transcript would not load, so it is reported here as an index entry to be confirmed rather than a fact.
ellen.lesson: The archive framed three absences as a mystery about emigration. At least one of them was a child's grave in St Paul's.

hannahGap.test: HANNAH SMITH at Berkeley, 1795–1815 — the same query that finds Hannah Saniger nothing.
hannahGap.result: Nineteen results, and the ONLY baptism collection that returns anything for Berkeley is England Births & Baptisms 1538-1975, the FamilySearch index. FindMyPast's own GLOUCESTERSHIRE BAPTISMS collection covers Bristol parishes but does not reach Berkeley at all.
hannahGap.verdict: So Berkeley's register after 1677 reaches this subscription through one partial index and no other. That index holds John Saniger's children of 1801, 1803 and 1808 and not his daughter of 1805. Hannah's baptism is not missing from the register; it is missing from the only transcription of it that money can currently buy.
hannahGap.next: Which makes the original Berkeley parish book, at Gloucestershire Archives, the one document left standing between this family and a fully evidenced English line.

lydia: And Lydia is still nobody's wife on paper. No John Saniger marries at Berkeley between 1792 and 1804, though his children are baptised there from 1801. The woman the tree calls Hannah's mother, and the seventy-year-old Lyddya Sinegar living in Hannah's house in 1841, remain joined by nothing but a surname and a household.
queensland: And Jabez and Zillah were not left behind either. Jabez married in Queensland in 1863 and was buried there in 1903; Zillah married in Queensland in 1871. They sailed with their parents, and the passenger register had them all along.
